<context_window_protection>
  <priority_instructions>
    Every byte a tool returns enters your conversation memory and costs reasoning capacity for the rest of the session. The context-mode tools let you do the work in a sandbox and surface only the derived answer — the raw bytes stay out. Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.
  </priority_instructions>

  <tool_selection_hierarchy>
    0. MEMORY: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(sort: "timeline")
       - On resume or compaction, query prior decisions, errors, plans, user prompts before asking the user — auto-captured session memory is searchable.
    1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.
    2. FOLLOW-UP: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(queries: ["q1", "q2", ...])
       - Multiple related questions about anything already indexed (your captures + session memory). Batch every question in one array; the ranking pipeline runs per-query and the round-trip cost is paid once.
    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.
  </tool_selection_hierarchy>

  <when_not_to_use>
    - You intend to PROCESS the output (filter, count, parse, aggregate) → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute or mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute. Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).
    - You want to analyze, summarize, or extract from a file → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file. Read stays correct when you intend to Edit the file (Edit needs the exact bytes in your conversation to match against).
    - WebFetch → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index; full network access, results indexed for mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search, raw page bytes never enter your conversation.
    - mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute and mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file for file writes → these run code in a subprocess and discard the sandbox FS; they are for analysis, processing, and computation only.
  </when_not_to_use>

  <file_writing_policy>
    File writes use the native Write or Edit tool — mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute, mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file, and Bash subprocesses do not persist edits to the host filesystem.
    Applies to all file types: code, configs, plans, specs, YAML, JSON, markdown.
  </file_writing_policy>

  <output_constraints>
    <artifact_policy>
      Write artifacts (code, configs, PRDs) to files. Return only: file path + 1-line description.
    </artifact_policy>
  </output_constraints>
  <session_continuity>
    Skills, roles, and decisions captured earlier in this session are a memory aid, not a standing order. Treat them as context that may help — the user's most recent message always takes precedence. If a captured directive conflicts with what the user now asks, follow the user; a past phrase does not bind you.
  </session_continuity>

  <ctx_commands>
    "ctx stats" | "ctx-stats" | "/ctx-stats" | context savings question
    → Call stats MCP tool, display full output verbatim.

    "ctx doctor" | "ctx-doctor" | "/ctx-doctor" | diagnose context-mode
    → Call doctor MCP tool, run returned shell command, display as checklist.

    "ctx upgrade" | "ctx-upgrade" | "/ctx-upgrade" | update context-mode
    → Call upgrade MCP tool, run returned shell command, display as checklist.

    "ctx purge" | "ctx-purge" | "/ctx-purge" | wipe/reset knowledge base
    → Call purge MCP tool with confirm: true. Warn: irreversible.

    After /clear or /compact: knowledge base preserved. Tell user: "context-mode knowledge base preserved. Use `ctx purge` to start fresh."
  </ctx_commands>

</context_window_protection>"}}

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

content.content:
=============== SESSION-HANDOFF ===============
# Session handoff — 2026-08-17/18

Written so a fresh Claude Code session, or Eric six weeks from now, can pick this up
without the originating conversation. Everything below was decided in a session that no
longer exists.

**Read `CLAUDE.md` first** — it loads automatically and carries the architecture. This
file carries the *reasoning*, and particularly the things that were tried and rejected,
so they are not re-litigated.

---

## Where this came from

Eric asked for agents covering four things: education slides, an internship curriculum,
research project ideas, and a way to capture questions that arise randomly.

**The founding decision was that those are not four projects.** Education, the
internship, and research all consume the same raw material — questions staff generate
constantly and lose immediately. So the architecture is one ledger feeding three
producers, tied together by the competency taxonomy. If a future change would split
them back apart, that undoes the central bet.

Two external inputs shaped the build:

- **Austin Marchese's WAT framework** (Workflows, Agents, Tools) — the layer split, and
  the rule that deterministic work belongs in `tools/` rather than in a prompt.
- **Boris Cherny's *Steps of AI Adoption*** — the verification rule (*build the
  verification, not the prompt*) and the adoption ladder in `docs/adoption-ladder.md`.

---

## Corrections already made — do not re-make these

Each of these was believed, then found wrong. They are recorded because the wrong
version is the intuitive one.

**1. GPS typical error is not recoverable from the session archive.**
An earlier plan was to compute TE for GPS metrics retrospectively. That is
methodologically wrong: TE requires repeated measurement of the *same* quantity with no
real change, and consecutive practices are different work, so real variation and sensor
error cannot be separated. It would need two units on one athlete simultaneously, or a
fixed repeated course. Retrospective TE **is** recoverable from ForceDecks, where weekly
standardized testing approximates test-retest. `tools/archive.py` says this in its
docstring and deliberately refuses to compute it.

**2. A CSV-parsing GPS tool was built here and then deleted.**
It parsed Catapult CSV exports. It was a worse rebuild of `erash11/DataBase_GPS_Reporting`,
which already pulls via the Connect v6 API into DuckDB with 3+ seasons of history.
Replaced by `tools/archive.py`, which reads that database. **Do not rebuild a GPS
ingest path in this repo.** (The deleted file was `gps.py`, in `tools/` — named here
without a full path so the reference checker does not flag a file that is gone on
purpose.)

**3. The adoption ladder's 1 → 2 analysis was rewritten for a solo department.**
The first version said the unlock was "a second person captures a question unprompted."
There is no second person — Applied Performance is one person. The ledger is a personal
memory system, and the "org that hasn't caught up" means coaches and adjacent
departments, not colleagues.

**4. Catapult arrives by API, not manual CSV.**
An early answer said manual export. It is the Connect v6 API via the separate repo.

**5. Cherny's self-verification loop belongs to the 1 → 2 transition, not step 3.**
Reconstructed from search summaries at first and placed wrongly; corrected against the
primary source. `tools/check.py` is therefore the named unlock for the step this
department is currently on.

---

## The department, as established

Gathered by direct questioning. Recorded in full in `context/department.md`.

- **One person.** Eric is the entire full-time department, covering every sport,
  football-anchored. 1–2 interns, **rolling starts, no cohort.**
- **No quiet window.** Overlapping seasons continuously. Prospective intervention
  studies are largely infeasible; the archive is the asset.
- **Biggest time sink: data wrangling.** Football GPS is automated; the remaining burn
  is elsewhere and **has not been pinned down.** Still an open question.
- **Stack:** Catapult (API, 3+ seasons, speed-band thresholds unchanged throughout —
  this makes the archive genuinely comparable). VALD ForceDecks, CMJ + IMTP, weekly.
  GymAware. Kitman Labs carrying medical/injury/availability plus some GPS/force-plate.
  Power BI being built now.
- **Testing is run by whoever is available**, so between-tester variation sits inside
  every number and our TE will exceed published values.
- **No wellness or sRPE collected.** Internal load does not exist as a variable.
  Anything built on sRPE-based ACWR is dead on arrival.
- **Only three education decks ever delivered** (CMJ, GPS, VBT). The cause is
  structural — no protected time — so `education-planner` proposes one deck at a time
  rather than a semester roadmap.
- **Nutrition and sport psych are separate departments** with frequent collaboration.
  Collaborators, not competency domains.

### The governance position

Baylor's AI approval covers general use but **does not address student-athlete data, and
nobody owns that ruling.** No external decision is coming. That makes the boundary AP's
own standing policy rather than a stopgap: `tools/` may process athlete data (plain
Python, local, no model sees it); agents get de-identified or aggregate output only.

---

## What is verified, and what is not

**Verified by execution:**
- `tools/reliability.py` against clean, noisy, and systematically-drifting fixtures —
  verdicts correct in each; the noisy set returned 11.3% CV, matching the published band
  for high-speed distance.
- `tools/check.py` against eleven deliberately injected defects — all caught, exit 1.
- `tools/archive.py` against a fixture matching the real schema and Catapult naming
  conventions.
- `tools/ledger.py` — capture, sequential IDs, stale detection, comment-stripping.

**Not verified:**
- **No agent has ever been run.** All five are untested prose. `check.py` verifies
  *form* — frontmatter parses, paths resolve — not behavior. The first real test is
  `/triage` against the five seeded ledger questions.
- `archive.py` has never seen a real DuckDB, only fixtures.

---

## The GPS pipeline review

`docs/gps-pipeline-review.md` records seven findings in `erash11/DataBase_GPS_Reporting`
at commit `cf6ca7f`. The pattern matters more than any single one: **`coach_report` has
30 tests, `gps_report` has none, and every substantive defect is in `gps_report`** while
`coach_report` already holds the correct approach for two of them.

Two are worth acting on:

- `total_player_load` stores `average_player_load` and is documented in that repo as not
  a usable volume metric — yet `gps_report` uses it for the KPI tile, position
  summaries, sort order, the email line, and baseline flagging.
- `get_rolling_baseline_df()` is the only query that does not scope. No day-type filter
  (walk-thrus pool with practices and desensitise the threshold) and no sport filter.

A committed Catapult JWT was also found in that repo. **Eric reviewed it and is not
concerned** — do not re-raise it.

---

## Curriculum work — current state

Branch `curriculum`, forked from the feature branch.

- `docs/curriculum/handbook.md` — v0 draft, addressed to the intern in second person.
  Onboarding is self-serve because rolling starts mean no orientation group exists.
- `docs/curriculum/modules.md` — eleven modules in four blocks, v0.
- `context/source/cpss-structure.md` — CPSS as a content spine and reference.

**Why the work is moving to a local terminal:** the CPSS PDFs and a reference school's
PowerPoints live on Eric's OneDrive, unreachable from a cloud container; `nsca.com` is
egress-blocked; and the deliverable is `.pptx` files that need to land somewhere usable.

### Settled: not exam prep

**This internship is not CPSS exam preparation.** CPSS is a content spine and a standing
reference, following the Clemson model — modules cover parts of the text and the text
stays available while working through them.

That voids the weightings question an earlier draft treated as blocking. Weightings are
exam-scoring artifacts; irrelevant here. `nsca.com` being unreachable stopped mattering
the moment the goal changed.

**Two axes are deliberately kept separate:** CPSS supplies module *content*, and
`context/competencies.md` supplies *assessment*. A module can teach CPSS Monitoring and
be assessed at AM L2. An earlier draft tried to make one taxonomy do both and it made
the mapping harder than it needed to be.

**The format decision matters more than the module list.** A module is a reading, a task
against real data, and a 20-minute discussion — **not a PowerPoint Eric builds.** Clemson
runs deck-per-module because Clemson has staff. The staff education series here produced
three decks and stopped; eleven intern decks would stop faster. Slides accumulate from
discussions that keep repeating, rather than being built up front.

---

## Honest risks

- **This may be over-built.** Roughly fifteen markdown files of doctrine for a
  one-person department. `curriculum-architect` is told to keep the intern program lean
  because an unmaintained program is worse than a simple one; that logic was never
  applied to this repo. Expect some of the prose to rot. The parts likely to survive are
  the tools, because they save time, and anything behind the verification gate.
- **Nothing has been run.** See above.
- **PR #1 is an unmerged draft.** All of this lives on branches.

---

## Open questions

1. Where does the wrangling time actually go, now that football GPS is automated?
2. University practicum requirements — hour counts, sign-off, mandated objectives.
   Hard constraints, not yet reflected in the handbook.
3. CPSS domain weightings.
4. Roster sizes per sport; which sports carry Catapult units; real calendar dates.
5. Whether the AM/OPS/COM default track is right, or should vary by intern.
6. Who signs off intern evidence when Eric is unavailable — the handbook currently
   assumes he observes everything, which will not survive camp.

content.content:
=============== MODULES ===============
# Module map

> **Draft v0.** Structure proposed before the CPSS PDFs were readable. Module *shape*
> should hold; module *content* needs checking against the real table of contents.
> Reading assignments are marked `<!-- TODO: chapter -->` rather than guessed.

Eleven modules across four blocks. An intern works through them individually — **there
is no cohort, so this is a sequence, not a schedule.** Someone arriving in week six
starts at Module 1 while the current intern is on Module 8. That is fine and is the
point.

---

## The format — read this before the module list

The single most important design decision here, and the one most likely to be
overridden by instinct.

**A module is not a PowerPoint Eric builds.** Clemson can run a deck-per-module program
because Clemson has staff. Applied Performance is one person with no protected time —
and the evidence is already in: the staff education series produced three decks and
stopped. Eleven intern decks would stop faster.

So each module is:

| Part | Who does the work | Time cost to Eric |
|---|---|---|
| **Read** — a section of the CPSS text | Intern | zero |
| **Do** — a task against our real data | Intern | zero once specified |
| **Discuss** — 20 minutes, no slides | Both | 20 min |
| **Evidence** — what it demonstrates | Intern produces, Eric signs | minutes |

**The task is the module.** Reading without doing produces someone who can discuss
monitoring and cannot run it. The discussion exists to catch misunderstanding, not to
transmit content — the text already did that.

**Slides accumulate rather than being built up front.** When a module's discussion has
happened three or four times and the same explanation keeps recurring, that explanation
is worth a deck — and by then it writes itself. Building eleven decks in advance is how
this dies in March.

---

## Block 1 · Foundations

Prerequisites for everything after. Do not reorder these.

### M1 — What Applied Performance is, and is not

**CPSS:** Training Theory and Process (role and scope) · **Assessed:** RTP L1, COM L1

The role, and its edges. Who decides what. Applied Performance supplies evidence; it
does not clear athletes, prescribe fueling, or interpret psychological state.

- **Do:** Sit in on one cross-functional conversation. Afterwards, write down each
  decision made and who owned it.
- **Evidence:** Can state where AP's remit stops in three specific situations.
- **Why first:** An intern who blurs these boundaries in week two creates a problem no
  competency makes up for.

### M2 — Every measure has error

**CPSS:** Monitoring, Needs Analysis · **Assessed:** DL L2 · **Reference:**
`context/measurement-standards.md`

Typical error, smallest worthwhile change, and the ordering rule: *is this bigger than
our noise* comes before *is this meaningful*.

- **Do:** Run `tools/reliability.py` against a real ForceDecks test-retest extract.
  Interpret the verdict for one athlete.
- **Evidence:** Correctly identifies one metric we report that cannot support the
  decision being asked of it.
- **The misconception it corrects:** that a number on a screen is a fact.

**This is the load-bearing module.** Everything downstream is worse without it, and it
is the one an intern is most likely to think they already understand.

---

## Block 2 · Monitoring

The department's strongest area, and where the data actually is.

### M3 — External load: what GPS measures

**CPSS:** Monitoring · **Assessed:** AM L1→L2

Metric definitions, speed bands, what total distance does and does not tell you. Why
thresholds must be locked before comparing across time.

- **Do:** Run `tools/archive.py profile` against the GPS archive. Report which columns
  are always zero, which are duplicates.
- **Evidence:** Explains each metric in the weekly report to someone who does not know
  the system.

### M4 — What we do not measure, and why

**CPSS:** Monitoring, Needs Analysis · **Assessed:** AM L2, DL L2

Internal load, wellness, sRPE — none collected here. The honest reasons: monitoring
burden is real, unpaid surveys decay, and a solo department cannot chase compliance.

- **Do:** Take one published study relying on sRPE-based ACWR. State what would need to
  change here to replicate it, and whether that is worth it.
- **Evidence:** Can identify when a question is unanswerable with our data, and say so
  rather than substituting a proxy.
- **Why this is a module and not a footnote:** interns arrive assuming everything is
  collected. Learning to name the gap is a competency.

===README===
# Source documents — drop uploads here

Raw material for the internship curriculum: existing handbooks, university practicum
requirements, prior intern job descriptions, evaluation forms, certifying-body
competency lists (NSCA, CSCCa, UKSCA), anything an intern is currently handed on day
one.

**Files here are inputs, not doctrine.** `curriculum-architect` reads them and writes
the curriculum to `docs/curriculum/`. Nothing here is authoritative on its own — where
a source conflicts with `context/department.md`, the department file wins, because it
records how the department actually operates rather than how a document says it should.

## Before uploading: athlete data

Per `context/department.md`, athlete-identifiable data does not enter a prompt. If a
document contains athlete names, medical status, injury history, or test results tied
to a person, **say so first** — redact it, or leave it out and describe what it
contains instead.

Two cases worth pausing over:

- **Past intern evaluations** name a real person. That person is staff rather than an
  athlete, so FERPA does not apply, but it is still someone's performance review.
  A deliberate decision, not an upload reflex.
- **Sample reports** used as teaching examples usually carry a live roster.

## What is most useful

Ranked by how much it actually changes the curriculum:

1. **University practicum requirements** — hour counts, supervisor sign-off, learning
   objectives the school demands. Hard constraints; everything else bends around them.
2. **Whatever interns are handed today** — even an informal one-pager. It reveals the
   implicit curriculum already in use, which is the real starting point.
3. **Prior evaluation forms** — they encode what has actually been assessed, which is
   usually narrower than what was intended.
4. **Certifying-body competency lists** — useful for external credibility, but written
   for a generic setting. `context/competencies.md` is deliberately behavioral and
   specific to this department; treat external lists as a cross-check, not a swap.
5. **Job descriptions** for roles interns are aiming at — the real target. An
   internship that does not move someone toward a hireable profile is a rotation, not
   a development program.

## What this worktree already knows

Branched from the AgentAssist feature branch, so the curriculum work starts with:

- `context/competencies.md` — eight domains, four behavioral levels
- `context/department.md` — solo department, 1–2 rolling interns, no cohort, no quiet
  window, football-anchored, wrangling as the biggest time sink
- `agents/curriculum-architect.md` — already told to keep the program lean, because a
  handbook built for a ten-intern cohort is overhead a solo supervisor will not maintain

Those constraints should shape everything here. If an uploaded document assumes a
cohort, a large staff, or protected time, the document is describing a different
department.

===CPSS-STRUCTURE===
# NSCA CPSS — content spine and reference

**Certified Performance and Sport Scientist.** Used here as a **content spine and a
standing reference**, following the Clemson model: modules cover different parts of the
text, and the text stays available while an intern works through them.

> **Decided: this internship is not CPSS exam preparation.** We follow the text's themes
> and ideas; we do not optimise for someone sitting the exam. This is a deliberate scope
> choice, not a gap.

## What that decision settles

**Domain weightings do not matter and are not worth chasing.** They are exam-scoring
artifacts. An earlier draft of this file treated missing weightings as blocking, on the
reasoning that an intern on a narrow track would be underprepared for a quarter of the
exam. With exam prep off the table, that concern is void. `nsca.com` being unreachable
from a cloud environment stopped mattering the moment the goal changed.

**One thing does survive from that analysis.** If the text devotes substantial space to
training theory and our modules skip it entirely, we are not actually following the
text's themes — we are cherry-picking the parts we already teach. Worth checking against
the real table of contents, but as a coverage question, not an exam-risk one.

## The four domains

1. **Training Theory and Process**
2. **Needs Analysis**
3. **Monitoring**
4. **Communication and Education**

Plus three crosscutting concepts spanning all four.
<!-- TODO: name them from the text. Low priority now. -->

## Two axes, deliberately not merged

The most useful thing to keep straight:

| Axis | Source | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Content** — what a module teaches, what to read | CPSS text | *What does an intern need to understand?* |
| **Assessment** — evidence and levels | `context/competencies.md` | *How do we know they can do it?* |

These are orthogonal. A module can take its content from CPSS *Monitoring* and be
assessed against **AM L2**. Do not collapse one into the other — an earlier draft tried
to make one taxonomy carry both jobs and it made the mapping harder than it needed to be.

## How the domains relate to ours

Reference only, now that neither is being fitted to the other.

| CPSS domain | Our domains | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Training Theory and Process | SP | Our thinnest coverage. Worth a module regardless, since the text treats it as foundational. |
| Needs Analysis | RM, DL | CPSS treats as one thing; we split it. |
| Monitoring | AM, NM | Our strongest, and where the department's data actually lives. |
| Communication and Education | COM | The field's own credential treats this as a full domain rather than a soft skill. Independent support for the emphasis the handbook already places on it. |

Nothing in CPSS maps to our **OPS** domain. That is not an oversight — pipeline
maintenance is a departmental reality rather than a professional competency. Keep OPS;
for this department it has the clearest return. Just do not expect the text to cover it,
which means **OPS modules are ours to write from scratch** while the rest have a source.

## Using the text

- **As a reference during modules**, not as assigned reading to be completed. An intern
  should know where in the text to look, which is a different skill from having read it
  cover to cover.
- **Practice questions** are a self-check on comprehension, not an assessment. Our
  assessment is behavioural (see the handbook). Someone can answer every practice
  question and still be unable to produce a usable load report.
- **Where the text and this department disagree, the department wins**, and the
  disagreement is worth teaching explicitly. A text written for the field in general
  will assume resources, staffing, and internal-load data we do not have.

# NSCA CPSS — content spine and reference

**Certified Performance and Sport Scientist.** Used here as a **content spine and a
standing reference**, following the Clemson model: modules cover different parts of the
text, and the text stays available while an intern works through them.

> **Decided: this internship is not CPSS exam preparation.** We follow the text's themes
> and ideas; we do not optimise for someone sitting the exam. This is a deliberate scope
> choice, not a gap.

---

## Verified against the real materials — 2026-08-18

Everything below the line was **read from the actual PDFs**, not inferred. Where this
file previously guessed, the guess is named so it is not re-made.

### Where the source files are

`context/source/` — copied in from
`~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/09_PRO_DEV/Courses/CPSS/`.

**They are gitignored** (`context/source/*.pdf`, `*.pptx`). Purchased NSCA material and

artifacts. An earlier draft of this file treated missing weightings as blocking, on the
reasoning that an intern on a narrow track would be underprepared for a quarter of the
exam. With exam prep off the table, that concern is void. `nsca.com` being unreachable
from a cloud environment stopped mattering the moment the goal changed.

**One thing does survive from that analysis.** If the text devotes substantial space to
training theory and our modules skip it entirely, we are not actually following the
text's themes — we are cherry-picking the parts we already teach. Worth checking against
the real table of contents, but as a coverage question, not an exam-risk one.

## The four domains

1. **Training Theory and Process**
2. **Needs Analysis**
3. **Monitoring**
4. **Communication and Education**

Plus three crosscutting concepts spanning all four.
<!-- TODO: name them from the text. Low priority now. -->

## Two axes, deliberately not merged

The most useful thing to keep straight:

| Axis | Source | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Content** — what a module teaches, what to read | CPSS text | *What does an intern need to understand?* |
| **Assessment** — evidence and levels | `context/competencies.md` | *How do we know they can do it?* |

These are orthogonal. A module can take its content from CPSS *Monitoring* and be
assessed against **AM L2**. Do not collapse one into the other — an earlier draft tried
to make one taxonomy carry both jobs and it made the mapping harder than it needed to be.

## How the domains relate to ours

Reference only, now that neither is being fitted to the other.

| CPSS domain | Our domains | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Training Theory and Process | SP | Our thinnest coverage. Worth a module regardless, since the text treats it as foundational. |
| Needs Analysis | RM, DL | CPSS treats as one thing; we split it. |
| Monitoring | AM, NM | Our strongest, and where the department's data actually lives. |
| Communication and Education | COM | The field's own credential treats this as a full domain rather than a soft skill. Independent support for the emphasis the handbook already places on it. |

Nothing in CPSS maps to our **OPS** domain. That is not an oversight — pipeline
maintenance is a departmental reality rather than a professional competency. Keep OPS;
for this department it has the clearest return. Just do not expect the text to cover it,
which means **OPS modules are ours to write from scratch** while the rest have a source.

## Using the text

- **As a reference during modules**, not as assigned reading to be completed. An intern
  should know where in the text to look, which is a different skill from having read it
  cover to cover.
- **Practice questions** are a self-check on comprehension, not an assessment. Our
  assessment is behavioural (see the handbook). Someone can answer every practice
  question and still be unable to produce a usable load report.
- **Where the text and this department disagree, the department wins**, and the
  disagreement is worth teaching explicitly. A text written for the field in general
  will assume resources, staffing, and internal-load data we do not have.

# Module map

> **Draft v0.** Structure proposed before the CPSS PDFs were readable. Module *shape*
> should hold; module *content* needs checking against the real table of contents.
> Reading assignments are marked `<!-- TODO: chapter -->` rather than guessed.

Eleven modules across four blocks. An intern works through them individually — **there
is no cohort, so this is a sequence, not a schedule.** Someone arriving in week six
starts at Module 1 while the current intern is on Module 8. That is fine and is the
point.

---

## The format — read this before the module list

The single most important design decision here, and the one most likely to be
overridden by instinct.

**A module is not a PowerPoint Eric builds.** Clemson can run a deck-per-module program
because Clemson has staff. Applied Performance is one person with no protected time —
and the evidence is already in: the staff education series produced three decks and
stopped. Eleven intern decks would stop faster.

So each module is:

| Part | Who does the work | Time cost to Eric |
|---|---|---|
| **Read** — a section of the CPSS text | Intern | zero |
| **Do** — a task against our real data | Intern | zero once specified |
| **Discuss** — 20 minutes, no slides | Both | 20 min |
| **Evidence** — what it demonstrates | Intern produces, Eric signs | minutes |

**The task is the module.** Reading without doing produces someone who can discuss
monitoring and cannot run it. The discussion exists to catch misunderstanding, not to
transmit content — the text already did that.

**Slides accumulate rather than being built up front.** When a module's discussion has
happened three or four times and the same explanation keeps recurring, that explanation
is worth a deck — and by then it writes itself. Building eleven decks in advance is how
this dies in March.

---

## Block 1 · Foundations

Prerequisites for everything after. Do not reorder these.

### M1 — What Applied Performance is, and is not

**CPSS:** Training Theory and Process (role and scope) · **Assessed:** RTP L1, COM L1

The role, and its edges. Who decides what. Applied Performance supplies evidence; it
does not clear athletes, prescribe fueling, or interpret psychological state.

- **Do:** Sit in on one cross-functional conversation. Afterwards, write down each
  decision made and who owned it.
- **Evidence:** Can state where AP's remit stops in three specific situations.
- **Why first:** An intern who blurs these boundaries in week two creates a problem no
  competency makes up for.

### M2 — Every measure has error

**CPSS:** Monitoring, Needs Analysis · **Assessed:** DL L2 · **Reference:**
`context/measurement-standards.md`

Typical error, smallest worthwhile change, and the ordering rule: *is this bigger than
our noise* comes before *is this meaningful*.

- **Do:** Run `tools/reliability.py` against a real ForceDecks test-retest extract.
  Interpret the verdict for one athlete.
- **Evidence:** Correctly identifies one metric we report that cannot support the
  decision being asked of it.
- **The misconception it corrects:** that a number on a screen is a fact.

**This is the load-bearing module.** Everything downstream is worse without it, and it
is the one an intern is most likely to think they already understand.

---

## Block 2 · Monitoring

The department's strongest area, and where the data actually is.

### M3 — External load: what GPS measures

**CPSS:** Monitoring · **Assessed:** AM L1→L2

Metric definitions, speed bands, what total distance does and does not tell you. Why
thresholds must be locked before comparing across time.

- **Do:** Run `tools/archive.py profile` against the GPS archive. Report which columns
  are always zero, which are duplicates.
- **Evidence:** Explains each metric in the weekly report to someone who does not know
  the system.

### M4 — What we do not measure, and why

**CPSS:** Monitoring, Needs Analysis · **Assessed:** AM L2, DL L2

Internal load, wellness, sRPE — none collected here. The honest reasons: monitoring
burden is real, unpaid surveys decay, and a solo department cannot chase compliance.

- **Do:** Take one published study relying on sRPE-based ACWR. State what would need to
  change here to replicate it, and whether that is worth it.
- **Evidence:** Can identify when a question is unanswerable with our data, and say so
  rather than substituting a proxy.
- **Why this is a module and not a footnote:** interns arrive assuming everything is
  collected. Learning to name the gap is a competency.

### M5 — Neuromuscular assessment

**CPSS:** Monitoring · **Assessed:** NM L1→L3

CMJ and IMTP. Outcome metrics versus strategy metrics — jump height can hold while
movement strategy degrades. Why cueing changes the result, and why "whoever is
available" running the test is inside our error.

- **Do:** Administer the battery under supervision. Then interpret one athlete's trace
  against their own history, not a group norm.
- **Evidence:** Runs the battery unsupervised with standardized cueing.

---

## Block 3 · Analysis and evidence

### M6 — Needs analysis

**CPSS:** Needs Analysis · **Assessed:** RM L2, AM L2

Sport demands, position demands, athlete profiling. What the sport actually requires
before deciding what to monitor.

- **Do:** Write a needs analysis for one position group in a sport that is *not*
  football.
- **Evidence:** Distinguishes what matters for the sport from what happens to be
  measurable.

### M7 — Reading the literature

**CPSS:** Needs Analysis · **Assessed:** RM L2, DL L2

Design, sample, primary outcome. External validity — most sport science is done on
recreationally trained young men, and whether it transfers to a D1 roster is a question,
not an assumption.

- **Do:** Appraise one paper. State plainly whether it transfers to our population.
- **Evidence:** Identifies a limitation the abstract does not mention.
- **Teach explicitly:** ACWR as contested rather than settled. Uncritical use is a
  competency failure, not a stylistic preference.

---

## Block 4 · Training theory, communication, operations

### M8 — Training theory and programme intent

**CPSS:** Training Theory and Process · **Assessed:** SP L1→L2

Dose and response, periodization, why a block is built the way it is. **Our thinnest
area** — no staff education has ever covered it — but the text treats it as foundational
and skipping it would mean not actually following the text.

- **Do:** Read one sport's current programme. Identify the intent of each block and
  state what would tell you it is working.
- **Evidence:** Reads a programme and explains its logic without being told.

### M9 — Communicating with coaches

**CPSS:** Communication and Education · **Assessed:** COM L2

An insight that does not change a decision was a hobby. One point per slide. Surviving
"so what?"

- **Do:** Take a finding and write the single sentence a coach would act on. Then ask a
  coach what would have to change before they trained someone differently — the
  decision-anchored SWC conversation from `measurement-standards.md`.
- **Evidence:** One slide that makes one point and survives pushback.

### M10 — Delivering education

**CPSS:** Communication and Education · **Assessed:** COM L3

The intern's own session to cross-functional staff. **Non-negotiable**, and scheduled
early enough that a second attempt is possible.

- **Do:** Spec and deliver a 5 Slides in 5 Minutes session. Topic from the ledger's
  TEACH entries, so it answers something someone actually asked.
- **Evidence:** Delivered, and handled the two hardest questions honestly — including
  "we don't know" where that was true.

### M11 — The data pipeline

**CPSS:** *no equivalent — ours to write* · **Assessed:** OPS L2→L3

Where each stream originates and lands. How it breaks. The weekly routine.

- **Do:** Run the weekly report end to end. Break it deliberately, then fix it.
- **Evidence:** Diagnoses and repairs a broken pipeline step unsupervised.
- **Why it matters here more than the credential suggests:** the intern who makes the
  Monday report happen without being asked is the one who pays for their own
  supervision.

---

## Sequencing

**Fixed:** M1 and M2 first, in that order. M2 gates everything analytical.

**Then largely flexible.** Order the rest around what the calendar is doing — M5 during
a testing block, M3 when GPS is live, M10 when there is an audience.

**M10 needs runway.** Schedule it by the midpoint so a second attempt fits.

A one-semester intern will not complete eleven modules to depth. **That is expected.**
Three or four to L3 and the rest to L1–L2 is the target from the handbook, and it is
better than eleven done shallowly.

---

## Open

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What this repository is

A **Claude Code plugin** for the Baylor Athletics Applied Performance department,
built on the WAT pattern (Workflows, Agents, Tools). Most of it is prompts, domain
doctrine, and a plain-text ledger; the `tools/` layer is real Python.

The governing principle, and the one to preserve when editing: **probabilistic AI
handles reasoning, deterministic code handles execution.** If a step has one correct
answer — a date stamp, a sequential ID, a standard deviation, a count — it belongs in
`tools/`, not in a prompt. Agents that reimplement tool work in prose are a
regression, even when the prose looks right.

## Layout

```
workflows/   markdown SOPs — objective, inputs, tools, steps, outputs, edge cases
agents/      roles and judgement — which workflow, what "done" means
tools/       deterministic Python, stdlib except archive.py --db
             ledger.py  capture/parse/IDs · reliability.py  TE, SWC, verdicts
             archive.py GPS archive audit  · check.py  the verification gate
commands/    slash-command entry points
context/     domain doctrine the agents load
ledger/      the question ledger (inbox + backlog)
docs/        education log, generated research briefs
```

## Athlete data: the tools layer is a privacy boundary

Baylor's approved AI path covers general use but does **not** address student-athlete
data. Until someone rules explicitly, athlete data is unapproved rather than
permitted-by-default (FERPA, possibly HIPAA).

This lands cleanly on the existing split, and it is the most useful consequence of
having a tools layer at all:

| Layer | Athlete data |
|---|---|
| `tools/` — deterministic Python, runs locally, no model involved | **Yes** |
| Agents and prompts | **No** — de-identified or aggregate only |

So automation of athlete data is not forbidden; it is `tools/` work. A wrangling script
that joins Catapult exports to ForceDecks output is fine. Pasting the resulting roster
into a prompt is not. When a question genuinely needs identifiable data in a prompt,
flag it and get a ruling rather than proceeding carefully.

## Verification — the definition of done

```bash
python3 tools/check.py
```

**Clean exit is the definition of done.** Any agent that writes to `ledger/`,
`docs/research/`, `agents/`, or `commands/` must run this before reporting finished
work, and must fix what it reports rather than explaining it away.

This follows Boris Cherny's rule — *give the agent a way to verify its work and quality
goes up 2–3×; build the verification, not the prompt.* It is why `check.py` exists as
a gate rather than as advice.

What it catches: duplicate or gapped Q-numbers, off-taxonomy routes/domains/statuses,
entries routed but never sharpened, PARK without a reason, missing required fields,
inbox lines that no longer parse (silently un-triageable captures), agent frontmatter
whose `name` disagrees with its filename, markdown references to files that do not
exist, tools that do not compile, and research briefs missing required sections.

Suites run individually: `check.py ledger`, `check.py plugin`, `check.py briefs`.

Warnings never fail the run; errors exit 1.

## Architecture

One ledger feeding three producers, tied together by a competency taxonomy.

```
ledger/inbox.md ──/triage──> question-triage ──> ledger/backlog.md
                                                  │
                            ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
                        TEACH                  STUDY                 ANSWER
                            │                     │                     │
                   education-planner      research-designer   analytics-feasibility
                            │                     │
                   five-slides-generator   docs/research/
                     (external skill)
                            └──────── curriculum-architect ────────┘
```

**`context/competencies.md` is the keystone.** Eight domain codes (`AM`, `NM`, `SP`,
`DL`, `RTP`, `COM`, `RM`, `OPS`) are the shared index across triage tagging,
education planning, and internship targets. Changing or renaming a domain code is a
breaking change — every agent references these codes and several files tabulate them.
Grep for the code before editing.

**`context/department.md` is load-bearing and incomplete.** It carries `<!-- TODO -->`
markers for facts only the department can supply (vendors, roster sizes, calendar
dates, compliance contacts). Agents are instructed to flag a blocking TODO rather than
substitute a plausible value. Preserve that instruction when editing agents — a
guessed fact about whether the AMS joins to GPS produces confidently wrong feasibility
calls downstream.

**`context/measurement-standards.md` is the analytical spine.** It encodes the ordering
rule that `analytics-feasibility` and `research-designer` must follow: establish the
noise floor (typical error vs. smallest worthwhile change) *before* assessing whether
a change is meaningful. This ordering is deliberately restated in both agents because
skipping to "is it meaningful" is the default behavior of both humans and LLMs.

## The inbox/backlog split

Two files with deliberately different friction, and the split is the core design bet:

- `ledger/inbox.md` — one line, no categories, no dedup, no cleanup. `/capture` must
  stay this cheap or people stop using it on a practice field.
- `ledger/backlog.md` — structured blocks with route, domain, feasibility, effort,
  `asked-count`.

Do **not** add validation, categorization, or duplicate-checking to `/capture`. Every
one of those is a reason to skip capturing, and the whole system dies at that step.
Duplicates are intentional signal — `asked-count` is the primary priority metric.

Entries are *moved* from inbox to backlog by triage, never deleted.

## Adding to the plugin

Decide the layer first:

| The thing is… | Goes in |
|---|---|
| A repeatable procedure with defined inputs and outputs | `workflows/` |
| Judgement, role, or "what done means" | `agents/` |
| Deterministic — one correct answer every time | `tools/` |
| A user entry point | `commands/` |
| Domain fact or doctrine | `context/` |

- **Agents** → `agents/<name>.md`, YAML frontmatter with `name`, `description`,
  `tools`. The `description` routes work to the agent, so write it as trigger
  conditions, not a job title.
- **Commands** → `commands/<name>.md`, frontmatter with `description`,
  `argument-hint`, `allowed-tools`. `$ARGUMENTS` interpolates user input.
- **Tools** → stdlib Python with an `argparse` CLI and JSON or plain-text output, so
  staff run them without a setup step. One exception: `archive.py --db` needs `duckdb`,
  which is already installed wherever the GPS pipeline runs. Its `--csv` path stays
  stdlib.
- Register nothing — `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` holds metadata only; agents and
  commands are discovered by directory.

Every new agent that touches data or study design must load
`context/measurement-standards.md` and `context/department.md`, and must call
`tools/reliability.py` rather than reasoning about measurement error in prose.

## Related repositories

**`erash11/DataBase_GPS_Reporting`** owns the football GPS data layer: Catapult
Connect v6 API client, DuckDB store (`gps_report/data/gps_history.duckdb`), bulk
historical import, the post-practice HTML report, and a coach report with XmR SPC
charts. AgentAssist reads that database; it does not duplicate the pipeline. An
earlier CSV-parsing tool here was removed once it became clear it was a worse rebuild
of that repo — reuse beats rebuild, and it applies to this plugin too.

Read that repo's `CLAUDE.md` before touching anything GPS — it records which Catapult
slugs are broken for this account, the mph/m-s conversions, and the
`average_player_load` trap described in `context/department.md`.

## External skill dependencies

These live on the user's claude.ai account, not in this repo:

- `five-slides-generator` — owns the "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" house format and the
  `.pptx` build. `education-planner` specs decks and hands off; it must not write
  decks itself.
- `design-academy-skill` — data visualization and dashboard principles.
- `articulation-skill` — explaining technical concepts to non-technical staff.

## Domain conventions

- Prefer **within-athlete** designs over between-athlete comparisons. Squad sizes
  (n = 15–110) make between-groups work underpowered and fragile; each athlete as
  their own control is the applied setting's structural advantage.
- Speed-band and metric-definition thresholds must be locked before any across-time
  comparison — redefining a band creates an artifactual step change.
- ACWR is taught as contested, not settled. Uncritical use is treated as a competency
  failure.
- Return-to-play clearance is a medical decision; Applied Performance supplies
  evidence only. Agents must not phrase output as a clearance recommendation.
- Athlete data is FERPA-covered and may be HIPAA-covered, and is **not** covered by
  Baylor's AI approval. See the privacy boundary above. Agents flag governance
  questions; they never rule on IRB or compliance.
- Applied Performance is **one person** covering every sport, with 1–2 rolling interns.
  Anything that costs Eric keyboard time is a tax on the entire department. Weight
  recommendations accordingly — his biggest time sink is data wrangling, which this
  plugin does not yet address.

## Git

Development happens on `claude/applied-performance-agents-quca93`.

1. **"Four domains" was wrong.** Those are exam-score buckets. The real text is **7 Parts, 31 chapters**.
2. **The old list skipped Parts 3, 5, and 6.** That is a third of the book.

## What I filled in

- All **11 module readings**, from the real chapter list.
- The **coverage answer**: what is left over is mostly Part 6, and that is nutrition, sport psych, and sports medicine. Other departments. Not a hole.
- **Two real gaps**: Ch23 Recovery/Sleep and Ch25 Environmental Stress (heat in Waco is real). I folded both into M4 instead of adding modules. Count stays at 11.

- `context/source/cpss-structure.md` — real chapter list, both corrections
- `docs/curriculum/modules.md` — v1, readings filled, coverage answered
- `docs/session-handoff.md` — update entry, open question 3 closed

Nothing is committed. It sits on the `curriculum` branch for you to look at.

**Keep the M4 fold, or split it out?**

- **Split it** — a 12th module for recovery and heat. More content, but one more thing to run.
